name: Blind loop syndrome (small intestinal bacterial overgrowth)

reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Presents with bloating, flatulence, abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea and, when severe, steatorrhoea and weight loss
Characteristically causes vitamin B12 deficiency because bacteria consume the vitamin, while folate is often normal or high as bacteria synthesise it
Fat malabsorption arises from bacterial deconjugation of bile acids, which impairs micelle formation, and may cause fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
It results from stasis or loss of the normal barriers to bacterial colonisation, for example surgically created blind loops, strictures, diverticula, dysmotility or loss of gastric acid
Hydrogen (and methane) breath testing after a carbohydrate load is a widely used non-invasive diagnostic approach, though jejunal aspirate culture is a reference standard
Correcting or bypassing the underlying anatomical or motility abnormality is important where feasible
Treatment uses antibiotic courses for bacterial overgrowth together with nutritional replacement, and cyclical antibiotics may be needed for recurrent disease
reference.pathophysiology: Blind loop syndrome, or small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, occurs when excessive numbers of colonic-type bacteria colonise the normally sparsely populated small intestine. Normal protective mechanisms include gastric acid, intact intestinal motility that sweeps the lumen, the ileocaecal valve and immune defences; anatomical stasis from a surgically created blind loop, strictures, fistulae or diverticula, or impaired motility, allows bacteria to proliferate. These bacteria deconjugate bile acids, impairing fat absorption and causing steatorrhoea, consume dietary vitamin B12 leading to deficiency, and synthesise folate. They also injure the mucosa and produce gas and toxic metabolites, giving rise to the diarrhoea, bloating and malabsorption that characterise the syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Inflammatory bowel disease, especially with strictures or fistulae
additionalInvestigations: Hydrogen and methane breath testing after a carbohydrate substrate
Jejunal aspirate culture where available as a reference test
Vitamin B12 and folate levels showing the typical pattern of low B12 with normal or raised folate
Assessment of fat malabsorption and fat-soluble vitamins
Imaging or endoscopy to identify a blind loop, stricture, diverticula or dysmotility
redFlags: Severe or neurological features of vitamin B12 deficiency
Symptoms suggesting an underlying stricture, fistula or malignancy
Failure to respond to antibiotics, prompting reassessment of the diagnosis and anatomy
reference.prognosis: Symptoms usually improve with antibiotic treatment and correction of deficiencies, but relapse is common when a fixed anatomical or motility abnormality cannot be corrected, and some patients need recurrent or cyclical therapy.
pitfalls: Diagnosing irritable bowel syndrome without considering bacterial overgrowth in at-risk patients
Overlooking the underlying anatomical or motility cause that perpetuates overgrowth
Failing to replace vitamin B12 and fat-soluble vitamins
Relying on a single breath test result given its limited sensitivity and specificity
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
American College of Gastroenterology guidance on small intestinal bacterial overgrowth
management: Antibiotic therapy (such as rifaximin, or rotating courses of tetracyclines with metronidazole) to reduce the bacterial overgrowth, given cyclically where relapse occurs
Correct or bypass the underlying anatomical stasis (blind loop, stricture, fistula or diverticula) surgically where feasible, and use prokinetics for dysmotility
Parenteral vitamin B12 replacement together with supplementation of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K
Nutritional support with correction of malnutrition and a modified-fat diet incorporating medium-chain triglycerides for steatorrhoea
Symptomatic control of diarrhoea and bloating
Monitor haematinics, nutritional status and symptoms for relapse, anticipating recurrent or cyclical treatment when a fixed abnormality cannot be corrected

Escalate: exclude stricture, fistula or malignancy; urgent B12 replacement
Hydrogen or methane breath test after carbohydrate; vitamin B12 and folate levels
Check fat-soluble vitamins; imaging or endoscopy for blind loop, stricture or dysmotility
Overgrowth shown, with low B12 and normal or high folate?
Antibiotic course such as rifaximin; B12 and fat-soluble vitamin replacement
